name: Northern Rhodesia
info: The British protectorate north of the Zambezi, ruled by the British South Africa Company until 1924 and then by the Crown, whose Copperbelt mines made it rich and which became independent as Zambia in 1964.

facts.founder: The British South Africa Company, which merged its two protectorates north of the Zambezi as Northern Rhodesia in 1911
facts.predecessor: Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia, the two British South Africa Company protectorates; the Lozi kingdom of Barotseland under Lewanika and the chiefdoms with which the company made treaties

t: Northern Rhodesia was formed in 1911 from two protectorates of the British South Africa Company, which ruled it until 1 April 1924, when the British Government took over its administration.
Large-scale copper mining on the Copperbelt began after 1924, financed mainly from the United States and South Africa, and by the end of the 1930s it was booming.
Its inclusion in the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953, against strong African opposition, hastened the campaign for majority rule that led to independence as Zambia in 1964.
dyk: Northern Rhodesia is the only country to have changed its name and flag during an Olympic Games: it entered the 1964 Summer Olympics as Northern Rhodesia and left the closing ceremony on 24 October as Zambia.
ev: The British South Africa Company merges Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia as Northern Rhodesia
On 1 April the British Government takes over the administration, with Herbert Stanley as governor and Livingstone as capital
A retrospective tax increase sets off a strike on the Copperbelt, and police shoot six Africans dead at Luanshya; the capital moves to Lusaka
African miners strike after European miners win higher pay, and troops of the Northern Rhodesian Regiment fire on them, killing 17
Northern Rhodesia joins the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland against strong African opposition
Kenneth Kaunda and the younger radicals leave the Congress of Harry Nkumbula and form the Zambia African National Congress
The governor declares a state of emergency on 12 March, bans the Zambia African National Congress and arrests Kaunda; the United National Independence Party is formed in October
On 24 October the country becomes independent as the Republic of Zambia, with Kaunda as President

sections.foundation:
The territory came under British control through Cecil Rhodes and his British South Africa Company. Rhodes, whose main interest lay south of the Zambezi, wanted the north held as cheaply as possible and sent emissaries to make treaties with chiefs. Joseph Thomson and Alfred Sharpe made treaties west of Nyasaland in 1890 and 1891. In Barotseland Lewanika, king of the Lozi, who wanted protection against internal unrest and Ndebele raids, was told by Frank Elliott Lochner that the company represented the British government, and on 27 June 1890 granted it an exclusive mineral concession in return for a subsidy and a promise of British protection that Lochner had no authority to give.

An Order-in-Council of 9 May 1891 placed the region under company administration, and its borders with Mozambique, Angola, German territory and the Congo Free State were fixed by treaties between 1890 and 1905; a Belgian expedition's agreement with Msiri in 1891 kept Katanga for the Congo Free State and left the Congo Pedicle. The company ran the area as two protectorates, Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia, recognised by Orders-in-Council of 1899 and 1900, with the Colonial Office ultimately responsible for their African populations. In 1911 it merged them as Northern Rhodesia, and their High Courts were joined as the High Court of Northern Rhodesia.
sections.socioeconomy:
Under company rule Northern Rhodesia was valued chiefly as a reservoir of migrant labour for Southern Rhodesia. Hut tax, extended across the territory between 1901 and 1913 and set at about two months' wages, was meant to force Africans into wage labour; in 1920 it was sharply raised, often doubled, to send more workers to mines such as Wankie. The railway reached the Congo border in 1909, and from 1912 to 1928 almost all of Katanga's copper went over it. European settlers were few, about 3,000 at the end of the First World War. Native Reserves were created in 1928 and 1929, about half the land along the main railway line was kept for Europeans, and by 1938 the reserves were overcrowded while much European land lay unused.

Copper transformed the economy after rich sulphide ores were found below the surface at Bwana Mkubwa in 1924. Roan Antelope at Luanshya was developed from 1926, Mufulira opened in 1930 and Nkana, at Kitwe, began commercial production with Roan Antelope in 1931, financed by Chester Beatty's Selection Trust, the American Metal Company and the Anglo American Corporation. The price crash of 1931 cost many miners their jobs and ended European hopes of a white dominion, but the mines recovered and by the end of the 1930s were booming. African miners lived under pass laws from 1927 and a colour bar kept the better jobs for Europeans.
sections.military:
The company judged the north better suited to an African than a European police force. The British South Africa Police at first patrolled North-Western Rhodesia; it was replaced by the Barotse Native Police, and North-Eastern Rhodesia formed a constabulary in 1903 whose NCOs and troopers were all African. Both were merged into the Northern Rhodesia Police, which in 1912 numbered only 18 Europeans and 775 Africans in six companies. Force was used against protest: a largely non-violent protest by the Gwembe Tonga against hut tax in 1909–10 had been severely suppressed.

The Copperbelt strikes brought the heaviest violence. In May 1935, after a retrospective tax increase, miners at Mufulira, Nkana and Roan Antelope struck; British South Africa Police were sent from Southern Rhodesia, and on 29 May police at Luanshya shot six Africans dead. In March 1940 African miners struck when they were refused the rise just conceded to striking European miners, and troops of the Northern Rhodesian Regiment fired on them, killing 13 at once and four more later. In the Second World War Northern Rhodesian units fought for Britain in the East African Campaign, the Battle of Madagascar and Burma, and the Ministry of Supply bought the mines' copper for the armed forces at set prices.
sections.governance:
Under the company an Administrator held powers like a governor's, some reserved to the High Commissioner for South Africa, advised by an Advisory Council of officials, to which five nominees of the European minority were added after 1917; there was no elected representation. The Northern Rhodesia Order in Council of 1924 created a governor, an Executive Council and a Legislative Council. Five unofficial members were first elected in 1926 by a European electorate, since electors had to be United Kingdom citizens with an income of £200 or property worth £250, which in practice excluded Africans. A nominated European member to represent African opinion was added in 1938, a Speaker replaced the governor in 1948, and from 1948 the African Representative Council recommended two African members.

Over Africans the government practised Direct Rule: District Officers, except in Barotseland, took away the chiefs' judicial powers and deposed troublesome ones. The Indirect Rule introduced in 1930 differed little in practice, since the Native Authorities had limited judicial and very limited financial powers; the Native Courts Ordinance of 1937 recognised native courts. In 1930 Lord Passfield's memorandum reasserted the paramountcy of African interests and ruled out further white minority governments. Advisory Provincial Councils followed in 1943, and an African Representative Council for the whole protectorate in 1946.
sections.impact:
Northern Rhodesia's copper made it valuable far beyond its borders. Katanga's copper was carried over the Rhodesian railway from 1912 until a Congolese line was finished in 1928, and the Copperbelt mines, financed from the United States and South Africa, drew in little British capital at first; in 1929 the British government encouraged a group of nine companies to finance Nchanga so that it would not fall under the control of an American cartel. In the Second World War Northern Rhodesian copper became a vital resource, and in 1949 the British South Africa Company agreed to give the government 20% of its revenues and to transfer its remaining rights in 1986.

The mineral wealth also drew the settler politics of the region northward. Southern Rhodesian politicians sought amalgamation to gain the Copperbelt, and Northern Rhodesian settlers, among them from 1941 Roy Welensky's Northern Rhodesian Labour Party, sought minority rule, alone or with the south. Against them Africans built their own institutions: independent churches such as the Ethiopian Church in Barotseland and the Watchtower movement rejected missionary control, and Welfare Associations of educated Africans, united in 1946 and renamed the Northern Rhodesia Congress in 1948, became the core of the national movement. Its leaders included two former teachers, Harry Nkumbula and Kenneth Kaunda.
sections.decline:
The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, created in 1953 after the Colonial Secretary Oliver Lyttelton dropped the condition of sounding out African opinion, was intensely unpopular with the African majority. Harry Nkumbula, who replaced Godwin Mbikusita Lewanika as head of Congress in 1951, and Kenneth Kaunda, its Secretary General from 1953, turned from seeking more representation to demanding majority rule, with boycotts against the colour bar. In October 1958 Kaunda and the radicals broke away to form the Zambia African National Congress. On 12 March 1959 the governor declared a state of emergency, arrested 45 of its members and banned it; Kaunda was sentenced to 19 months for conspiracy, although no credible evidence was produced.

The United National Independence Party, formed in October 1959, took Kaunda as leader on his release in January 1960. The Monckton Commission concluded in 1960 that the Federation could be kept only by force or by massive changes in racial legislation. Under a complex franchise devised by Iain Macleod with Welensky, the elections of October 1962 gave the party 14 seats for about 60% of the votes; Nkumbula's Congress then joined it in a coalition under Kaunda as Prime Minister. The Federation was dissolved on 31 December 1963, the party won 55 of 75 seats in the election of 1964, and on 24 October 1964 the country became the Republic of Zambia.

summary: Northern Rhodesia was formed in 1911 from the British South Africa Company's protectorates north of the Zambezi and ruled by the Crown from 1924. Its Copperbelt copper mines made it valuable to Britain and to the settlers of the south, its settlers sought minority rule, and African opposition to the Federation of 1953 led to independence as Zambia in 1964.

A. Keppel-Jones, Rhodes and Rhodesia: The White Conquest of Zimbabwe 1884–1902 (McGill-Queen's Press, 1983)
I. Brownlie, African Boundaries: A Legal and Diplomatic Encyclopaedia (Hurst & Co., 1979)
R. I. Rotberg, The Rise of Nationalism in Central Africa: The Making of Malawi and Zambia, 1873–1964 (Harvard University Press, 1965)
P. E. N. Tindall, A History of Central Africa (Frederick A. Praeger, 1968)

pointDescs.1911: The British South Africa Company merges its two protectorates as Northern Rhodesia; the main railway line has crossed to the Katanga mines.
pointDescs.1912: Full-scale copper production begins in Katanga, shipped over the Rhodesian railway until 1928; the Northern Rhodesia Police has 18 European and 775 African members.
pointDescs.1920: Hut tax is sharply raised, often doubled, to drive more Africans to work in the Southern Rhodesian mines, causing unrest.
pointDescs.1924: The British Government takes over on 1 April with Herbert Stanley as governor; rich copper sulphide ores are found at Bwana Mkubwa.
pointDescs.1926: Five unofficial members are first elected to the Legislative Council by the European minority; the Roan Antelope mine is developed at Luanshya.
pointDescs.1931: Roan Antelope and Nkana begin commercial production, but the copper price crashes and many miners are dismissed.
pointDescs.1935: The Copperbelt strike against a retrospective tax rise ends with six Africans shot dead at Luanshya; the capital moves from Livingstone to Lusaka.
pointDescs.1939: The Bledisloe Commission rules out immediate amalgamation with Southern Rhodesia; by the end of the 1930s the copper mines are booming.
pointDescs.1940: Troops fire on striking African miners, killing 17; an inquiry recommends better pay and conditions.
pointDescs.1943: African miners gradually gain jobs once reserved for Europeans; the Ministry of Supply pays half the cost of expanding Nchanga, and Provincial Councils are set up.
pointDescs.1946: An African Representative Council is formed, and the Welfare Societies unite in a federation that becomes the Northern Rhodesia Congress in 1948.
pointDescs.1949: The British South Africa Company agrees to give the government 20% of its revenues; a Victoria Falls conference without Africans proposes federation.
pointDescs.1953: Northern Rhodesia joins the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland despite a general strike called by Congress in March.
pointDescs.1959: A state of emergency is declared on 12 March and the Zambia African National Congress banned; the United National Independence Party is formed in October.
pointDescs.1962: Elections under Macleod's complex franchise lead to a coalition of the United National Independence Party and Nkumbula's Congress under Kaunda.
pointDescs.1963: The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland is formally dissolved on 31 December.
pointDescs.1964: The United National Independence Party wins 55 of 75 seats, and on 24 October the country becomes the Republic of Zambia.

notes: The article gives the railway reaching the Congo border in 1909 in one place and the main line crossing to Katanga in 1911 in another; both are kept where they belong (1909 the border, 1911 the end of primary construction).
The Barotse Native Police is dated 1902 with 'other sources' giving 1899 or 1901; it is left undated.

Rotberg's book is listed in the article's bibliography as if it were a journal article ('Journal of the International African Institute', with Harvard University Press); it is given here as the Harvard book.
The strength curve is a judgement: the peak (1953) reflects the copper economy and the enlarged institutions rather than any single dated event; the article does not measure output by year.
The Murder of Lilian Burton (May 1960) and the details of the 1959 franchise are left out for length.
